name: Trigeminal Autonomic Cephalalgia

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD-3) Criteria for Trigeminal Autonomic Cephalalgias

criteria.description: Recurrent unilateral headache attacks localized to the trigeminal nerve distribution
Ipsilateral cranial autonomic symptoms such as conjunctival injection, lacrimation, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, eyelid edema, forehead and facial sweating, miosis, or ptosis
Attacks lasting from seconds to hours depending on subtype (e.g., cluster headache attacks last 15-180 minutes)
Attacks occurring from once every other day up to 8 times per day
No better explanation by another diagnosis or secondary cause

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of recurrent unilateral headache attacks with ipsilateral cranial autonomic symptoms and attack duration consistent with TAC subtype, excluding other causes
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Subtypes include cluster headache, paroxysmal hemicrania, SUNCT, and others with specific criteria

pathognomonic.symptomName: Unilateral severe orbital or temporal headache
searchTerms: one-sided severe headache near eye or temple
unilateral orbital or temporal head pain
intense headache on one side of head
red eye and tearing on same side as headache
eye redness and watering on headache side
nasal stuffiness or runny nose on headache side
sweating on forehead and face on headache side
dislike of noise with headache attacks

occasional.symptomName: Sensory disturbances in trigeminal nerve distribution
searchTerms: tingling or numbness in trigeminal nerve area
sensory changes in face nerve distribution
pain affecting both sides of head
autonomic symptoms on opposite side of headache
temporary weakness on one side during attacks

imaging: MRI brain to exclude secondary causes such as tumors or vascular malformations
High-resolution MRI may show hypothalamic activation on functional imaging during attacks
other: Autonomic function testing may reveal ipsilateral parasympathetic activation
Response to indomethacin in paroxysmal hemicrania subtype

distinguishingFeatures: Migraine typically has longer duration attacks (4-72 hours)
Bilateral or unilateral headache without strictly ipsilateral autonomic symptoms
Presence of aura and photophobia/phonophobia more prominent
Brief, electric shock-like facial pain without prominent autonomic symptoms
Lack of restlessness or agitation during attacks

redFlags: Signs of secondary headache such as fever, weight loss, or systemic illness
references: International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (ICHD-3), 2018
May A, Schwedt TJ, Magis D, et al. The International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (beta version). Cephalalgia. 2013
Goadsby PJ, Lipton RB, Ferrari MD. Migraine—current understanding and treatment. N Engl J Med. 2002
